articles.title: This Game Was Labeled A Success. Its Developer Laid Off 85% Of Staff 2 Months After Release.
articles.description: In June, Netflix released an officially licensed FIFA World Cup game , and while it was not a critical success, Netflix management later singled it out as a successful release . Now, however, the studio behind the game, Refactor Games, has enacted a round of mass layoffs affecting the majority of the studio. Cofounder Nathan Burba told GamesBeat that the studio has laid off 85% off its staff. This amounted to about 80 people, according to Insider Gaming . The studio's co-owner, Delphi Interactive, was said to have pulled funding after the launch of the game in June. Affected developers were reportedly notified on Friday, July 31. The laid-off developers reportedly received no severance pay, though the last day was a payday. Netflix continues to grow its games business. The Netflix FIFA game, which is called FIFA World Cup Launch Edition , allows people to play on their TV or computer with up to four people. The game features all 48 teams, 1,238 players, and 16 stadiums from the tournament. The game received poor review scores, with VGC saying it's a "woefully undercooked companion" to the World Cup. During Netflix's latest earnings call, management said FIFA World Cup Launch Edition and the horror game Unhinged were two of company's "most successful" launches ever for cloud games on TV. Netflix did not share any specific datapoints that speak to their success, however. Despite some initial stumbles, Netflix remains interested and invested in the gaming space for the long term, seeing it as a major growth-driver. Recently, Netflix reported that some of its gaming efforts have grown by 600% , while also informing investors that it's still early days.

articles.title: Mystery swirls as Sean Duffy's million-dollar reality show vanishes into thin air
articles.description: Three months after it was unveiled with fanfare in the Oval Office, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's reality TV road trip series still hasn't released a single episode despite millions in donations from the very industries he regulates. Duffy, his wife Fox News host Rachel Campos-Duffy, and their nine kids allegedly filmed "The Great American Road Trip" over seven months, crisscrossing the country in a project pitched as celebrating America's 250th birthday and offering families a wholesome alternative to modern life, The Bulwark's Will Sommer noted on Monday evening. "To love America is to see America," Duffy said, describing the show's motto during a promotional appearance alongside President Trump. The five-part series was originally slated to premiere on YouTube in June, timed to Fourth of July festivities and Trump's separate Freedom250 celebration. Instead, summer is more than half over with nothing released, and the nonprofit behind the project, run by former travel-industry lobbyist Tori Barnes, has repeatedly declined to explain the delay, only promising the show is coming "in the coming weeks." The financing has drawn its own scrutiny. Boeing and Toyota each donated $1 million to sponsor the series, according to the Wall Street Journal, joined by Shell, Royal Caribbean, United Airlines and Comcast — all companies with business before Duffy's department. One travel company reportedly refused to buy in based on the ethics concerns. Sen. Patty Murray (D-WA) formally asked DOT's inspector general to investigate, while the watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington filed its own complaint alleging Duffy accepted improper travel benefits from sponsors his agency oversees. The Transportation Department maintains no taxpayer money funded the Duffy family's involvement, describing the trip as part of Duffy's official duties.
